title: Move Semantics
summary: Copying a large object duplicates its data. **Moving** transfers the data out of an object that is about to disappear, by handing over a few pointers. **Rvalue references**, written `T&&`, bind to such objects, and `std::move` lets you mark one as movable.
markdown:
## Copying versus moving A deep copy of a million-element vector allocates a new block and copies a million elements. Sometimes that is exactly what you need. Often the source is a temporary that is about to be destroyed anyway, and duplicating its data only to throw the original away is wasted work. ``` COPY: build an identical house and furnish it identically ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ furniture │ ── copy ──▶ │ furniture │ both are full └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ MOVE: hand over the keys ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ (empty) │ ── keys ──▶ │ furniture │ the old one is left empty └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ ``` ```cpp std::vector a(1'000'000, 7); std::vector b{ a }; // copy: allocate, then copy a million ints std::vector c{ std::move(a) }; // move: take over a's block. Instant. a is now empty. ``` ``` before the move: a ──▶ [7 7 7 ... 7] after the move: a ──▶ (nothing) c ──▶ [7 7 7 ... 7] ``` A move transfers **ownership** of the resource. Nothing is duplicated. ## Lvalues and rvalues When is it safe to take an object's contents? When nothing else will use that object afterwards. The language captures this with two **value categories**, introduced briefly in [[4.03 References]]. | | lvalue | rvalue | |---|---|---| | Has a name or a lasting location | Yes: `x`, `v[0]`, `*p` | No: `5`, `x + 1`, `makeVector()` | | Can have its address taken | Yes | No | | Exists after the expression ends | Yes | No: it is a temporary | | Safe to take from | No: other code may still use it | Yes: nobody else can refer to it | The full picture has finer categories, covered in [[11.01 Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding]]. This simpler view is enough to use move semantics correctly. ## Rvalue references An ordinary reference `T&` binds to lvalues. An **rvalue reference** `T&&` binds to rvalues. That gives overloading a way to tell them apart. ```cpp #include #include void take(const std::string&) { std::cout << "lvalue: must leave it alone\n"; } void take(std::string&&) { std::cout << "rvalue: may take its contents\n"; } int main() { std::string name{ "Ada" }; take(name); // lvalue take(std::string{ "Bo" }); // rvalue take(std::move(name)); // rvalue: you marked it return 0; } ``` ## Writing the move operations A class gets move semantics from two more special member functions, both taking `T&&`. ```cpp class Buffer { public: // constructor, destructor and copy operations as in 7.03 Buffer(Buffer&& other) noexcept : m_data{ std::exchange(other.m_data, nullptr) }, m_size{ std::exchange(other.m_size, 0) } { } Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& other) noexcept { if (this != &other) { delete[] m_data; m_data = std::exchange(other.m_data, nullptr); m_size = std::exchange(other.m_size, 0); } return *this; } private: int* m_data{}; std::size_t m_size{}; }; ``` `std::exchange(a, b)` stores `b` into `a` and returns the old value of `a`. Here it takes the pointer and leaves `nullptr` behind in one step. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["source owns the data"] -->|"move constructor"| T["target owns the data
source holds nullptr"] T --> D["source is destroyed:
delete[] nullptr does nothing"] ``` Leaving the source empty is essential. Its destructor will still run, and it must not release what the target now owns. | | Move constructor | Move assignment | |---|---|---| | Signature | `T(T&& other) noexcept` | `T& operator=(T&& other) noexcept` | | The target | Is being created | Already exists and must release its old resource first | > [!important] Mark move operations `noexcept` > When a `std::vector` reallocates, it moves its elements only if their move constructor is `noexcept`. Otherwise it **copies** them, to stay safe if something throws half-way. Forgetting `noexcept` silently makes vectors of your type slow. ## `std::move` does not move `std::move(x)` is a cast. It turns `x` into an rvalue reference and does nothing else. The actual transfer happens in whichever move constructor or move assignment operator that cast then selects. After being moved from, an object is in a **valid but unspecified state**: ```cpp std::string s{ "hello" }; std::string t{ std::move(s) }; s = "new value"; // fine: assigning gives it a known state again ``` | With a moved-from object you may | You should not | |---|---| | Destroy it | Assume anything about its contents | | Assign it a new value | Use it as though it still held the old value | ## Where moves happen without being asked | Situation | Example | |---|---| | Returning a local object | `return result;` | | Passing a temporary | `v.push_back(std::string{ "x" });` | | Inside library code | `std::sort`, `std::swap`, vector reallocation | This is why returning a vector by value has been cheap all along. > [!warning] Do not write `return std::move(local);` > Plain `return local;` lets the compiler construct the result directly in the caller, skipping even the move ([[6.02 Constructors]]). Adding `std::move` prevents that and makes the code slower. ## The Rule of Five The Rule of Three becomes the **Rule of Five**: ``` destructor · copy constructor · copy assignment · move constructor · move assignment If you declare any one of them, declare all five: define, = default or = delete each. ``` The compiler's own rules make this important: | If you declare | The compiler no longer generates | |---|---| | A destructor or a copy operation | The move operations: "moves" quietly become copies | | A move operation | The copy operations: the class becomes move-only | And the Rule of Zero still beats both: use members that already move correctly, and declare nothing. ## Move-only types Some types can be moved but not copied, because having two copies would make no sense: `std::unique_ptr`, `std::thread`, file streams. ```cpp std::unique_ptr a{ std::make_unique(5) }; std::unique_ptr b{ a }; // error: copying is deleted std::unique_ptr c{ std::move(a) }; // fine: ownership is transferred ``` ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `std::move` actually do? - It moves the object's memory to a new address - It copies the object, then destroys the original + It casts to an rvalue reference; it moves nothing itself - It sets the object to an empty state > `std::move` is only a cast. The actual moving happens in the move constructor or move assignment it allows to be selected. ? Why should a move constructor be `noexcept`? - Because moves cannot fail - Because the compiler rejects it otherwise + So `std::vector` moves, rather than copies, when it grows - So it can be called on const objects > A vector must keep its elements safe if something throws while growing. It only moves elements when the move is `noexcept`. ? What can you safely do with a moved-from `std::string`? - Read its old contents, which are still there + Destroy it or assign it a new value - Nothing; using it in any way is undefined behaviour - Only print it > A moved-from string is valid but its contents are unspecified. Giving it a new value or letting it be destroyed is fine. ? Why must a move constructor leave the source empty? - So the source can be reused without changes - Because the source is deleted immediately - So that copying it later is faster + The source's destructor still runs and must free nothing > After stealing the pointer, set the source's pointer to `nullptr` so its destructor does not free the target's memory. ```
ideas:
1. Write a `Tracer` class that prints from every special member function. Push tracers into a vector with and without `reserve`, return one from a function, and swap two.
2. Remove `noexcept` from the move constructor and watch vector reallocation start copying.
3. Time copying against moving a `std::vector<std::string>` holding a million strings.

cards.a:
It casts to an rvalue reference; it moves nothing itself

`std::move` is only a cast. The actual moving happens in the move constructor or move assignment it allows to be selected.

cards.q: Why should a move constructor be `noexcept`?
cards.a:
So `std::vector` moves, rather than copies, when it grows

A vector must keep its elements safe if something throws while growing. It only moves elements when the move is `noexcept`.

cards.q: What can you safely do with a moved-from `std::string`?
cards.a:
Destroy it or assign it a new value

A moved-from string is valid but its contents are unspecified. Giving it a new value or letting it be destroyed is fine.

cards.q: Why must a move constructor leave the source empty?
cards.a:
The source's destructor still runs and must free nothing

After stealing the pointer, set the source's pointer to `nullptr` so its destructor does not free the target's memory.
